title: Rom 8:33 forensic: God who justifies vs accusation
source_text: XX. Similiter sensu forensi accipiunt multi Ecclesiae Romanae interpretes verba Pauli, Rom. 8. 33. Quis accusabit adversus electos Dei? Deus est qui justificat. Sic enim scribit ad hunc locum Toletus; Justificandi verbum in hoc loco, in ea significatione accipitur, quae est opposita antitheto, nempe condemnationi, ut idem sit hoc loco justificare, ac justum pronunciare, sicut judex sua sententia innocentem absolvit & pronunciat. Qua ratione quoque eundem locum exponit Pererius, ut idem etiam antea docuerat, referente Andrea Riveto in Summa Controversiarum, Tractatu 4. quaest. 1. Adamus Sasbout; Deus est qui justificat, id est, qui a peccatis & intenta accusatione absolvit. Quae verba retinuit Estius in Commentario.
pass_a_gloss: Likewise many interpreters of the Roman Church take Paul's words in a forensic sense, Rom. 8:33. Who shall accuse against God's elect? It is God who justifies. For thus Toletus writes on this place: The verb of justifying in this place is taken in that signification which is opposite to the antithesis, namely condemnation, so that to justify here is the same as to pronounce just, as a judge by his sentence absolves and pronounces the innocent. In which way Pererius also explains the same place, as Adamus Sasbout had also taught before, according to Andreas Rivetus in Summa Controversiarum, Tract. 4 q. 1: It is God who justifies—that is, who absolves from sins and from the accusation brought. Which words Estius retained in his Commentary.
pass_b_english: Rom 8:33: many Roman interpreters read justify forensically against accusation/condemnation.
Toletus, Pererius, Sasbout/Estius: judge-pronouncing the elect just.
